title: Chukat: the red heifer (Numbers 19)
hook: a ritual that purifies the impure and defiles the pure; tradition says even Solomon couldn't explain it

segments.voice: Yesterday, Aaron's staff put out buds, blossoms and ripe almonds overnight. Your line was the staff blossoms.

Why is the sky blue? Why do we have to? Why? Why? A small child can keep that up until the grown-up in the room runs out and says, because. Grown-ups tend to hope that with enough study, everything eventually has a because. Then comes this week's portion, Chukat, and the ritual it opens with is one that Jewish tradition itself says nobody has fully explained. A rare red cow, burned to ash. The ash makes people pure. And the people who prepare it become impure. A law with no because.
screen: `WHY? WHY? WHY?` → `A RARE RED COW, BURNED TO ASH.` → `A LAW WITH NO BECAUSE.`

segments.voice: The ritual, in paraphrase, goes like this. Find a red heifer, a young cow, completely red, with no blemish, that has never worn a yoke. She is slaughtered outside the camp and burned, with cedar wood, hyssop and scarlet thread thrown into the fire. Her ashes are kept and mixed with fresh water. Anyone who has touched a dead body is sprinkled with that water on the third day and the seventh, and becomes pure again. Then the twist: the priest who prepares it, and the one who burns it, become impure themselves, until evening. The same ashes that cleanse one person make another unclean. The chapter opens with the words chukat ha-Torah, the statute of the Torah. A chok, in the rabbis' vocabulary, is a law given without a stated reason, alongside mishpatim, laws anyone could work out, like don't steal. A midrash says King Solomon, famous for his wisdom, understood every law but this one, and quoted his own words from Ecclesiastes: I said, I will be wise, but it was far from me. Another midrash tells of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai. A non-Jew asks him about the ritual, and he gives a clever answer. Afterward his students say: you pushed him off; what do you tell us? He says, in paraphrase: the dead don't make impure, and the water doesn't make pure. It is a decree, and we keep it. Jewish thinkers have held different views since. Maimonides held that every commandment has a purpose, even when we can't see it. Others treat the chok as a lesson in trust. Both keep the law.
screen: `ASHES THAT CLEANSE, AND DEFILE.` · `CHOK: A LAW WITH NO STATED REASON.` · `EVEN SOLOMON: IT WAS FAR FROM ME.` · `IT IS A DECREE, AND WE KEEP IT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something you've never been able to explain: a loss, a person you love who does something you can't fathom, a question about God or about yourself. Don't try to solve it now. Hold it the way you'd hold a stone in your hand, and say to yourself, I don't understand this, and it's still here.
Chok. A statute, a law given without a stated reason. The red heifer is the classic chok: ashes that make one person pure and another impure.
Your line: not everything explains itself. I don't know yet is an honest answer. Day four hundred fifty-six, done.

howItsDone: Besides the weekly reading of Chukat, the red heifer chapter is read again on Shabbat Parah, a special Sabbath before Passover, recalling the purification once needed before the festival.

original.note: Hebrew: statute, a decree; the portion Chukat takes its name from chukat ha-Torah, the statute of the Torah (Numbers 19:2).

chat.says: Why do the red heifer's ashes make some people pure and others impure?
options: Tradition calls it a chok, a law without a stated reason; even Solomon found it far.
Because the ashes only work for priests, and make everyone else impure.
The Torah explains the reason right there in Numbers nineteen, plainly.
chat.meaning: The red heifer is the classic chok. A midrash says Solomon found it far from him, and Rabban Yochanan said: it is a decree, and we keep it.

chok.meaning: a statute: a law given without a stated reason

mishpatim.meaning: laws anyone could work out, like don't steal

Ecclesiastes.meaning: a biblical book of wisdom, linked by tradition to Solomon

Maimonides.meaning: a medieval scholar and thinker, also called Rambam

sources.ref: Maimonides, Guide for the Perplexed III:26

notes: Bamidbar Rabbah 19:3 (Solomon and Ecclesiastes 7:23) and 19:8 (Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai: 'the dead do not defile and the water does not purify; it is a decree'); confirm references. Also found in Pesikta de-Rav Kahana 4.
Ecclesiastes 7:23 is paraphrased, not quoted from JPS 1917.
Yoma 67b on chukim vs mishpatim; the red heifer appears in the list of chukim in some parallels (e.g. Rashi on Numbers 19:2). Confirm.
Maimonides' view: Guide III:26 holds all commandments have reasons in general; he discusses the red heifer specifically elsewhere (III:47). Confirm the citation.
Who exactly becomes impure (the priest, the one who burns it, the one who gathers the ashes) per Numbers 19:7–10; script names the priest and the one who burns it.
